claim: Opus 4.5 initially scored only 42% on CORE-Bench due to grading bugs -- rigid numeric matching that penalized correct answers in a different decimal format, ambiguous task specs, and stochastic tasks that were impossible to reproduce exactly -- and jumped to 95% after fixing the bugs and using a less constrained scaffold.
stance_target: eval scores should never be taken at face value without reading transcripts and auditing grading logic for bugs
quoted_support: Opus 4.5 initially scored 42% on CORE-Bench, until an Anthropic researcher found multiple issues: rigid grading that penalized "96.12" when expecting "96.124991...", ambiguous task specs, and stochastic tasks that were impossible to reproduce exactly. After fixing bugs and using a less constrained scaffold, Opus 4.5's score jumped to 95%.

claim: SWE-bench Verified scores for frontier LLMs rose from roughly 30-40% to over 80% within about one year, approaching saturation, meaning the benchmark now provides shrinking signal for further capability improvement.
stance_target: capability evals eventually saturate and must be replaced or extended to retain diagnostic value
quoted_support: LLMs have progressed from 40% to >80% on this eval in just one year... As evals approach saturation, progress will also slow, as only the most difficult tasks remain.

claim: pass@k (probability of at least one success in k trials) and pass^k (probability all k trials succeed) diverge sharply as k increases: pass@k approaches 100% while pass^k falls toward 0%, so the correct metric depends on whether the product needs one success (pass@k) or consistent reliability every time (pass^k).
stance_target: non-determinism in agent evaluation requires choosing the metric that matches the product's reliability requirement
quoted_support: If your agent has a 75% per-trial success rate and you run 3 trials, the probability of passing all three is (0.75)³ ≈ 42%... By k=10, they tell opposite stories: pass@k approaches 100% while pass^k falls to 0%.

claim: Teams should start eval suites with only 20-50 simple tasks drawn from real failures, because early in agent development each change has a large, clearly detectable effect, making small sample sizes sufficient.
stance_target: practical roadmap for building rigid evals from zero without over-investing upfront
quoted_support: We see teams delay building evals because they think they need hundreds of tasks. In reality, 20-50 simple tasks drawn from real failures is a great start.

claim: Grading an agent's exact tool-call sequence rather than its final outcome produces overly brittle evals, because agents regularly find valid approaches evaluation designers did not anticipate -- e.g. Opus 4.5 'failed' a tau2-bench flight-booking task by discovering a policy loophole that was actually a better outcome for the user.
stance_target: evaluating agents by rigid step-sequence matching rather than outcome-based grading
quoted_support: Opus 4.5 solved a 𝜉2-bench problem about booking a flight by discovering a loophole in the policy. It “failed” the evaluation as written, but actually came up with a better solution for the user... We've found this approach too rigid and results in overly brittle tests, as agents regularly find valid approaches that eval designers didn't anticipate.

claim: METR discovered misconfigured tasks in its time-horizon benchmark that asked agents to optimize to a stated score threshold while grading actually required exceeding it, penalizing models (like Claude) that followed the stated instructions and rewarding models that ignored the stated goal.
stance_target: eval grading bugs can systematically penalize instruction-following and invert the intended signal
quoted_support: METR discovered several misconfigured tasks in their time horizon benchmark that asked agents to optimize to a stated score threshold, but the grading required exceeding that threshold. This penalized models like Claude for following the instructions, while models that ignored the stated goal received better scores.

claim: Shared state between eval trials (leftover files, cached data, visible git history from prior runs) can give an agent an unfair advantage or cause correlated failures from infrastructure flakiness rather than true agent performance, so each trial must run in an isolated, clean environment.
stance_target: evaluation harness isolation is a prerequisite for valid, reproducible agent eval results
quoted_support: For example, in some internal evals we observed Claude gaining an unfair advantage on some tasks by examining the git history from previous trials.
